spark.main: One spark can lead to many possible futures. Project Ember is about exploring them faster.
talkingPoints: Let the animation breathe for about three seconds before speaking.
We are Project Ember: an adaptive wildfire surrogate.
Our goal is to go from simulating one future to exploring thousands.
Built this weekend on two NVIDIA GB10 nodes, orchestrated end to end with CIQ Fuzzball.
spark.interaction: No clicks needed. The ember lands, the fire spreads, and alternative fronts flash in cyan. The logo appears at about 6 s. Press → once the logo is up.
spark.evidence: Opening visual is an architectural illustration from the deck's own toy spread model, not simulator output (badge bottom-left).
spark.transition: But why does one spark have so many futures? Because conditions change.

humanProblem.main: The same starting point can produce very different simulated outcomes when conditions change.
talkingPoints: Wildfire threatens ecosystems, communities, infrastructure and livelihoods.
Watch the same ignition under four condition sets: wind direction, wind speed, fuel moisture.
The burned footprint near the structures changes every time. These are illustrations, not forecasts.
humanProblem.interaction: The scene cycles through condition presets automatically. Press → to reveal the closing statement: 'When conditions change, the questions multiply.'
humanProblem.evidence: Illustrative only; condition panel values drive the toy model and are labeled as such.
humanProblem.transition: A physics simulator answers exactly one of these questions at a time.

oneSimulation.main: A simulation is one answer to one set of assumptions. Covering the uncertainty takes many runs.
talkingPoints: On the left: one deterministic run with its input assumptions.
Each uncertain input we vary multiplies the number of runs: 1, then 3, then 9, then 27.
A simulated trajectory is a model of what could happen under assumptions, not a record of what will happen.
oneSimulation.interaction: Press → twice to grow the scenario tree one level at a time.
oneSimulation.evidence: Conceptual diagram. Branch counts show combinatorics, not measured workloads.

computeChallenge.main: Each question we ask adds another independent simulation job.
talkingPoints: Scenario requests pile up faster than a fixed pool of workers can drain them.
This is normalized and conceptual: no timings are shown here because none are claimed.
So the question becomes: what if the physics could be approximated?
computeChallenge.interaction: Let the queue fill for about 5 s, then press → to reveal the question.
computeChallenge.evidence: Normalized conceptual animation. Measured runtimes appear only on the Performance slide.

meetEmber.main: Ember is a pipeline: physics teaches, AI learns, Fuzzball coordinates, and we explore.
talkingPoints: Simulation generates examples. Examples become a dataset. A U-Net-style surrogate learns from it.
We evaluate against held-out simulator outputs. Fuzzball runs every stage as one workflow on our two GB10 nodes.
Each status chip shows what is implemented and what is proposed.
meetEmber.interaction: The pipeline draws itself. Click 'Neural surrogate' to open its card (role, inputs, outputs, compute, status), then click 'Fuzzball orchestration'.
meetEmber.evidence: Status chips come from snapshot.components. Until confirmed they read 'unconfirmed'.
meetEmber.transition: Before the science, here's the stack we built it on.

physicsEngine.main: First, we let physics teach. The simulator produces the ground truth the surrogate learns from.
talkingPoints: Name the simulator exactly as configured (ForeFire, or our simplified simulator, as the badge states).
Inputs: initial burned area, wind, fuel, moisture and slope layers. Output: burned-area masks over time.
Use the scrubber to show progression.
physicsEngine.interaction: Press play, then drag the time scrubber. Toggle 'Environment layers' and 'Progression lines'.
physicsEngine.evidence: With a recorded replay ingested, frames are simulator output (orange badge). Otherwise the viewer shows a labeled illustrative stand-in.
physicsEngine.transition: Each of those frames becomes a training lesson.

simulationToData.main: Every completed simulation becomes supervised training examples: input channels in, future mask out.
talkingPoints: One snapshot splits into aligned channels: burned mask, wind U/V, fuel, moisture, slope.
The target is the burned-area mask at a fixed horizon later.
We split by scenario, not by frame, so test scenarios are never seen in training.
simulationToData.interaction: Press → to explode the snapshot into channels, then again to show the dataset split.
simulationToData.evidence: Split counts come from data/manifest.json. Thumbnails are illustrative unless real samples are ingested.
simulationToData.transition: A neural surrogate learns from those pairs, and Fuzzball runs the whole experiment.

neuralSurrogate.main: A lightweight U-Net learns the mapping from conditions to the next fire extent.
talkingPoints: The encoder compresses spatial context, and the decoder rebuilds a full-resolution mask.
Skip connections keep fine edges of the fire front.
The spec panel reads from model metadata: parameter count, resolution, training config, device.
neuralSurrogate.interaction: Toggle 'Architecture / Prediction' at the top right. Prediction view shows real held-out predictions when ingested.
neuralSurrogate.evidence: All numbers come from model metadata and the checkpoint. A dash means not yet ingested.
neuralSurrogate.transition: Training and simulation have to run somewhere. Here's the cluster.

twoNodes.main: Two GB10 nodes, one continuous experiment: simulation produces while training consumes, then both nodes fine-tune the surrogate together.
talkingPoints: Planned architecture: Node A generates simulation shards, and Node B trains and evaluates.
Once the base surrogate is trained, both GB10s join for distributed fine-tuning: one model, data-parallel across Node A and Node B, with gradients synchronized between them.
Fuzzball Orchestrate coordinates dependencies, and shards move through a Fuzzball volume. Both nodes run RLC Pro AI 9.8 and Fuzzball Substrate.
Switch to Verified Execution to show what the logs actually recorded, including placement.
twoNodes.interaction: Start in 'Planned architecture', then click 'Verified execution'. If logs are ingested it shows real job placement. Otherwise it says so.
twoNodes.evidence: Verified view is built only from Fuzzball workflow logs (snapshot.workflow).
twoNodes.transition: Here's how we told Fuzzball to do that: the workflow itself.

fuzzball.main: Fuzzball turned the experiment into a recorded, dependency-aware run we can replay and reproduce.
talkingPoints: Each bar is a recorded job, with start, end, state and node.
Arrows show dependencies. Training starts only when its data exists.
Fuzzball orchestrates. It does not optimize the model.
fuzzball.interaction: Hover a bar for job details. Point out overlap between simulation and training if present.
fuzzball.evidence: Timeline is reconstructed from recorded workflow logs. It is labeled 'Recorded playback', never live.
fuzzball.transition: So did the AI actually learn the physics?

momentOfTruth.main: On held-out simulated scenarios, here's how closely the surrogate matches the simulator, including where it misses.
talkingPoints: Left: simulator reference. Middle: surrogate prediction. Right: error map (orange = over-predicted, cyan = missed).
Read the IoU, precision, recall and F2 for the held-out split.
Show a hard case on purpose. Honesty about failure modes is part of the result.
This is fidelity to simulation, not real-world forecast skill.
momentOfTruth.interaction: Click through the scenario selector, including the weakest example.
momentOfTruth.evidence: metrics/results.json via snapshot.fidelity. Per-example metrics are recomputed from masks when masks are provided.
momentOfTruth.transition: Accuracy is half the story. Did we save compute?

performance.main: We report three separate accelerations, and training cost on its own.
talkingPoints: Surrogate acceleration: simulator runtime vs neural inference per scenario.
Parallel throughput: one node vs two nodes.
Workflow acceleration: sequential vs overlapping pipeline.
We never multiply these into one headline number. Training cost is shown separately, so the comparison is honest.
performance.interaction: Point at each of the three cards in turn. Any card without measurements shows 'Awaiting'.
performance.evidence: Each card cites snapshot.benchmarks.source. Speedups are computed only when both measurements exist.
performance.transition: So here's how Ember measures up.

computeUnlocks.main: More compute means more scenarios, and an ensemble shows where outcomes agree and where they don't.
talkingPoints: One footprint, then many footprints, then an agreement map.
Agreement is the fraction of ensemble members that burn a cell. It is not a calibrated probability.
This is a proposed extension unless an ensemble result is ingested (see badge).
computeUnlocks.interaction: Drag 'Ensemble size' from 1 to 24, then toggle 'Agreement heatmap'. Optionally select individual members.
computeUnlocks.evidence: Marked as proposed future work and illustrative unless snapshot.ensemble exists.
computeUnlocks.transition: So what did we actually build?

conclusion.main: We didn't replace physics. We made it reusable.
talkingPoints: Read the checkmarks: only evidenced contributions are marked complete.
Point at 'Built with': Fuzzball, CIQ, NVIDIA, Lenovo and VAST, the hackathon stack we built on.
Next: real environmental data, physics-informed learning, adaptive simulation requests, larger ensembles.
Quantum-enhanced probability estimation is a future research direction, not part of Ember today.
Close: Project Ember, from one simulation to a scalable scientific-AI workflow.
conclusion.interaction: Press → once to bring back the ember and logo for the close. Leave it on screen for questions, and open Explore mode (E) for deep dives.
conclusion.evidence: Contribution status derives from snapshot evidence. Future items are badged 'Proposed'.

hackathonStack.main: Ember uses the whole hackathon stack: NVIDIA GB10 hardware, CIQ's RLC Pro AI, and Fuzzball as the backbone.
talkingPoints: Bottom up: 2 × Lenovo ThinkStation PGX with NVIDIA GB10, running RLC Pro AI 9.8 with the CUDA stack ready on first boot.
Fuzzball Substrate runs our containers on both nodes, Orchestrate schedules them, and volumes carry shards and checkpoints between stages.
We drove it through the Fuzzball CLI, web UI and MCP server.
Each chip says how we used that layer. Green means used, and logs upgrade it to verified.
hackathonStack.interaction: Layers build bottom-up. Click 'Fuzzball Orchestrate', then 'Fuzzball volumes' to show what's provided vs how Ember uses it.
hackathonStack.evidence: Environment facts are cited to the organizers' SC26 Hackathon Introduction deck. Usage status comes from data/verified/ecosystemUsage.json, and only Fuzzball logs upgrade it to 'verified'.
hackathonStack.transition: Now the science, starting with the physics.

fuzzfile.main: The entire experiment is one declarative Fuzzball workflow, which is why it's reproducible and scales across both nodes.
talkingPoints: ① A persistent Fuzzball volume is shared by every job on both nodes.
② Simulation fans out as a task-array: one scenario shard per task.
③ depends-on with status RUNNING lets the dataset build and training start while simulation is still producing. That's our producer–consumer overlap.
④ Training and evaluation request nvidia.com/gpu, so Orchestrate places them on a GB10 GPU.
We validate, start, watch and pull logs with the Fuzzball CLI.
fuzzfile.interaction: Press → three times to step through the four highlights, or click any callout.
fuzzfile.evidence: Until the team's real Fuzzfile is ingested this shows a reference template written to the documented v4 syntax (labeled). Once ingested, the real file is shown verbatim.
fuzzfile.transition: And here is what happened when we ran it.

judgingCriteria.main: Ember was built against all four official criteria, and the deck shows evidence for each.
talkingPoints: Technical execution: a complete simulate → learn → evaluate system, recorded as a Fuzzball workflow.
Ecosystem utility: NVIDIA GB10, CIQ RLC Pro AI and the full Fuzzball platform, each with its usage status.
Value and impact: faster what-if exploration for wildfire research, with honest limits.
Innovation: a physics-trained surrogate plus producer–consumer overlap across two nodes.
judgingCriteria.interaction: Sweep left to right across the four columns. A green check means an ingested artifact backs it.
judgingCriteria.evidence: Criteria text is quoted from the organizers' deck (pp. 3, 5). Checks are derived from the snapshot, never typed in.
judgingCriteria.transition: So here's where Ember goes next.

idea.main: Let physics teach, let AI learn: a simulator makes labeled examples, a neural surrogate learns from them.
talkingPoints: ForeFire is a real fire-spread physics simulator. It is accurate, but each run answers one 'what if' and costs CPU time.
Each run becomes a labeled example: conditions in, where and when the fire arrives out.
A U-Net learns that mapping on the GPU, so new scenarios can be answered in one forward pass. And we run simulation and training at the same time across two nodes.
idea.interaction: The three stages and the loop build in on their own.
idea.transition: So what did we actually feed it?

data.main: Real ForeFire simulations on real terrain, with a strict held-out test set.
talkingPoints: We prepared about 26,000 candidate conditions and kept 2,880 completed ForeFire simulations: 2,400 train, 300 validation, 180 test.
Each sample is a 320 by 320 grid of 40-meter cells, about 13 km square, with 19 input channels: fuel, moisture, slope, wind including a mid-run shift, and the ignition.
The model predicts two things over 60 minutes: which cells burn and when the fire arrives. The test set is never used to train or pick the model.
data.interaction: Let the split bar and fact tiles animate in.
data.transition: Here's how well the model learned it.

surrogateResults.main: On 180 simulations it never saw, the surrogate matches the physics reasonably well and errs on the cautious side.
talkingPoints: Precision 0.78: when it says a cell burns, it is usually right. Recall 0.55: it misses some burned area. Dice 0.65, IoU 0.48.
Arrival time is off by about 7 minutes on average over a 60-minute horizon.
It trained in about 11 minutes on a single GPU and the whole model is under 2 MB.
To be clear: this is agreement with the simulator, not real-world forecast accuracy.
surrogateResults.transition: Getting the system to scale was the hard part.

journey.main: Most of our time went into making physics and AI run together on real hardware. Four problems stood out.
talkingPoints: We couldn't reach the Fuzzball cluster off-site, so we built and proved each stage in small test runs first and staged the Fuzzball workflow for the on-site GB10 nodes.
ForeFire and PyTorch lived in incompatible Python environments, so we built a launcher that gives each its own runtime on the same node.
Our first full two-node run failed: the merge step rejected a duplicate label. That's the validator doing its job. We fixed the shard assignment, kept the strict check, and the next run passed.
A shared storage mount refused permission, so we moved to node-local scratch with hash-checked handoffs.
journey.interaction: The four test runs appear left to right, failure included, then the four fixes.
journey.evidence: Runs 1–4 on Nov 15; run 3 failed at the merge step.

twoNodeRun.main: Two nodes simulated and trained at the same time, merged verified labels, then fine-tuned one model across both GPUs.
talkingPoints: Phase one: on each node, ForeFire ran on the CPUs while the surrogate trained on the GPU, overlapping about 7 seconds on each node in this short run.
Then a barrier: we verified 126 fresh labels and merged them into training. Validation and test stayed untouched.
Phase two: one model, two GPU ranks, PyTorch DDP over NCCL. Both ranks ended with byte-identical weights. The whole job took 1 minute 40 seconds.
This was a short proof run; we're not claiming a speedup yet.
twoNodeRun.interaction: Press → to build: ① both nodes, ② verify + merge, ③ distributed fine-tuning and the summary stats.
twoNodeRun.evidence: Two-node test run on Nov 15 (run 4); DDP summary and per-node phase summaries.
twoNodeRun.transition: So where does that leave us?
